entries.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker Inference now supports GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which divides one GPU into hardware-isolated partitions so you can run a different model in each or take a right-sized fraction of a newer accelerator. This post shows how two optional API fields place one model per partition, and what we measured against a whole older GPU.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints

When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator.

This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An 

ml.p4d.24xlarge
has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach.

Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did.

One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components, the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned.

What customers do today, and why each option falls short

If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices.

Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not.

Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use.

Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have.

Why MIG

NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:

  • Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
  • Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
  • Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
  • No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
  • Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
  • Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.

Partitioning has boundaries worth knowing up front. The maximum number of partitions depends on the accelerator and never exceeds seven. MIG itself only allows a layout to change while its partitions are idle, and on SageMaker AI that means choosing a layout when you create the endpoint. A model that needs more than one GPU still needs whole devices. Within those boundaries, you get the isolation of separate GPUs without dedicating one to each model.

Partitioning without the platform work

Until now, getting MIG meant running the Kubernetes stack yourself. GPU partitioning on Amazon SageMaker AI removes that step: you pick a partition profile for your model, and SageMaker AI handles GPU configuration, placement and scaling. You get hardware-isolated GPU sharing on a managed endpoint, without having to run the platform underneath it.

Salesforce has been part of this work from the start, helping define the requirements and validating the initial implementation.

“NVIDIA MIG partitions a single GPU into multiple isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources. Salesforce sees this as an important capability because many inference workloads do not require an entire GPU. MIG would allow us to consolidate workloads safely, significantly improve GPU utilization, reduce inference costs, and maintain predictable performance and strong isolation.

This capability would help us scale AI Inference more efficiently across different use cases. Salesforce has helped define requirements, validated the initial solution. We are now preparing to validate the solution with representative production workload and demonstrate strong customer demand with AWS. We believe MIG support would deliver meaningful technical and business value for enterprise customers.”

— Richard Chang, Software Engineering Architect, Salesforce

How it works

GPU partitioning adds two optional fields to API calls you already make. There are no new API operations, no new resource types, and no new AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) actions, and an endpoint that omits both fields behaves exactly as it does today.

AcceleratorPartitionLayouts
goes on a production variant in 
CreateEndpointConfig
and declares how each accelerator is divided:

An A100 has seven compute slices to divide. The preceding layout uses all seven, so each of the eight A100s on the p4d instance carries three partitions and the endpoint provides 24, eight of each type.

The carve applies uniformly. One layout entry describes how one accelerator is divided, and every accelerator on every instance in the variant is divided the same way. The list isn’t positional, so an entry doesn’t map to a specific GPU.

AcceleratorPartitionType
goes on an inference component and selects which partition the model runs on:

Each component copy occupies one partition of the requested type. With eight partitions of each type on the instance, raising 

CopyCount
places additional copies on free partitions. This is useful for a small model serving high concurrency, where a single process leaves the GPU waiting on requests.

NumberOfAcceleratorDevicesRequired
is always 1 here. With a partition type set it means one partition rather than one accelerator. 
NumberOfCpuCoresRequired
and 
MinMemoryRequiredInMb
still describe host CPU and host memory, because GPU memory comes from the partition type.

Invocation doesn’t change. 

InvokeEndpoint
addresses a model by inference component name, and the partition it occupies never appears in the request.

Partitioning happens while the endpoint is provisioned. When it reaches 

InService
every accelerator is carved and the partitions are empty, which is a valid state as components land on them afterward. In our testing, carving accelerators added roughly 17 seconds to provisioning. The rest of the time is the usual instance launch and container pull.

Partition profiles by GPU

The profiles available to you are a property of the GPU, so start by finding out which GPU your instance type carries and look it up in NVIDIA’s supported MIG profiles, which is the authority on the full profile set and the combinations valid on one device.

Instance familyAcceleratorGPU memoryGranularity (compute / memory)Available partition profilesMax partitions per GPU
P4dNVIDIA A10040 GB7 / 8mig-1g.5gb, mig-1g.10gb (see driver note), mig-2g.10gb, mig-3g.20gb, mig-4g.20gb, mig-7g.40gb7
P5NVIDIA H10080 GB7 / 8mig-1g.10gb, mig-1g.20gb, mig-2g.20gb, mig-3g.40gb, mig-4g.40gb, mig-7g.80gb7
G7NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell32 GB2 / 2mig-1g.16gb, mig-2g.32gb2
G7eNVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition96 GB4 / 4mig-1g.24gb, mig-2g.48gb, mig-4g.96gb4

Read the profile name as compute units followed by GPU memory: 

mig-3g.40gb
takes three compute units and 40 GB. The granularity column is what limits a layout. An A100 and an H100 divide into sevenths on compute and eighths on memory, while G7 divides into halves and G7e into quarters. Profile names differ between GPUs even where the slice counts match, so don’t carry a layout from one instance family to another without checking it against this table.

Within those limits you have real choice. On a P4d or P5 you can carve seven of the smallest profile, or two 3g partitions, or the 4g plus 2g plus 1g layout used in the earlier example, or take the whole device as one. On a G7e you can take four of the smallest, or two 1g beside a 2g, or two 2g, or one whole device. On a G7, either two partitions or one.

The 3g profile is the one to know, because its two dimensions don’t match: it takes three of the seven compute units but four of the eight memory units. Two of them fill the GPU and nothing else will fit beside them.

The high-level rule: Every profile in your layout must be one your GPU offers, and the compute and memory units your profiles add up to must not exceed what one device provides. Both are checked when you create the endpoint configuration, and either one failing is a rejection rather than a fallback to a whole accelerator.

Driver note for P4d: mig-1g.10gb requires an R525 or newer NVIDIA driver, and the default P4d image ships 470.256.02. Request it on the default image and the carve fails without an error naming the profile. Set 

InferenceAmiVersion
to 
al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1
on the production variant to get an image on the 580 driver line, which offers it.

Choosing a layout for your workload

Choosing well is a separate question from choosing a layout that is merely accepted. A partition hands you compute and memory in fixed proportions, and the two do different jobs during inference.

Compute units are what you need for prefill. Prefill reads the prompt and builds its representation. This is the compute-heavy phase, and it scales with the streaming multiprocessors, and so the TFLOPs, your partition holds. The longer your inputs and the more prompts arriving at once, the more it governs how quickly you return a first token.

Memory units are what you need for decode and for capacity. Generating tokens re-reads the model weights on every step, so decode is bounded by memory bandwidth rather than by math, and memory also caps how much KV cache you can hold. That cap in turn sets the context length you can serve and how many sequences you can serve concurrently.

Almost no real workload exercises only one of these, so the goal isn’t to pick a dimension but to choose a combination that supports your use case. Choose a profile whose proportions cover your heaviest phase while leaving the other adequately served. On the compute side, what matters is how long your prompts are and how many arrive at once. On the memory side, it’s your output length, your context window, and your concurrency.

Memory is the easier of the two to underestimate, because a partition has to hold three things and not just the model: the weights, which for an 8B model at FP16 are about 16 GB. The KV cache, sized for the context length and the number of concurrent sequences you intend to allow, which is the term people leave out and the one that grows with traffic. And 1–2 GB of runtime overhead for the CUDA context and the serving process. Add those up before choosing a profile, because a partition sized to the weights alone will load the model and then fail under load, or quietly serve a much shorter context than you configured. For a concrete reference point, that same 8B model at FP16 comfortably serves an 8,000-token context on a 40 GB partition.

Where MIG adds the most value

A portfolio of small and mid-size models – The direct case. Fine-tuned variants, embedding models, rerankers, and classifiers that each leave most of an accelerator unused now share one.

Multi-tenant model serving – When you host a model per customer, MIG gives you a hardware boundary between them: a process in one partition can’t read another partition’s memory or take its throughput. Scope the claim accurately, though. Models on the same instance still share host CPU, system memory, storage, networking, and endpoint routing, so partitioning is an isolation mechanism for the GPU and not a complete tenancy boundary.

Multi-stage pipelines on one instance – A transcription model, a diarization model, and a language model, or an embedder, a reranker, and a generator. Each stage is a separately addressable component on its own partition, and a network hop between stages disappears.

A small model in the request path – A safety classifier or guardrail model that has to run on every request but cannot justify an accelerator, with predictable latency because it isn’t time-slicing against the main model.

Challengers and canaries – Run a candidate model on a small partition beside the model serving production traffic instead of standing up a second endpoint.

Performance: A slice of a newer GPU against a whole older one

In addition to bin-packing, the other benefit you get is granularity on high-end GPUs: more GPU options to deploy a model onto, and the choice of which one is yours. Every supported accelerator becomes several sizes rather than one, so the practical way to think about it is that each profile is a GPU option in its own right, sitting alongside the whole accelerators you already choose between. That matters most when you are considering a larger or newer instance type, because moving up stops being all-or-nothing: you can take as much or as little of that bigger GPU as your workload needs, at any of the sizes it publishes, instead of paying for the whole accelerator.

To see whether that pays off, we compared one 

mig-3g.40gb
partition of an H100 against one whole, uncarved A100-40GB. The two have comparable GPU memory, which makes it a clean way to see how powerful a slice of a more advanced instance can be.

We used genai-bench to generate load, driving both endpoints from the same client so the GPU is the only variable. Both sides ran Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on production SageMaker real-time endpoints, one model replica each, with an identical container image, tokenizer, and client configuration. Both were invoked through the SageMaker AI native OpenAI-compatible route. We swept five traffic shapes, written D(input tokens, output tokens) and ranging from short prompts to long-context summarization, each across a concurrency ladder from 2 to 512.

Four things stand out.

  • The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
  • Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
  • On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an 
    ml.p4d.24xlarge
    and $63.296000 per hour for an 
    ml.p5.48xlarge
    in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
  • At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

Treat this as a case-by-case comparison, not a verdict. The useful mental model is to regard the available GPU fractions as GPU types in their own right. List them alongside whole accelerators, work out what your traffic actually demands of compute and of memory, and compare them on your own workload. For high-concurrency, long-input traffic the partition won on both performance and cost here. For short-input or low-concurrency workloads the whole A100 remained cheaper. Partitioning isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. It gives you more sizes to choose from, so you can pick the one that fits your workload.

What to know before you commit to a layout

Partitioning changes the shape of an endpoint, and a few properties are worth understanding before you design one.

A component’s partition type is fixed for the life of that component. Moving a model to a different profile means creating a new component. Changing the endpoint’s carve means a new endpoint and a traffic migration, because updating an endpoint configuration doesn’t re-carve hosts that are already running. This makes partitioning a good fit for a stable portfolio and a poor one for a mix you reshuffle daily.

A requested profile has to exist in the endpoint’s layout. There is no fallback to a whole accelerator, so a component asking for a profile the variant didn’t declare is rejected.

Partitioning applies to real-time inference on inference component endpoints. Serverless endpoints and heterogeneous instance pools aren’t supported, and asynchronous invocation cannot address an inference component, so async workloads are out of scope.

You’re billed for the full GPU instance, as you are today. Partitioning raises how much of that instance you can use. It doesn’t change its hourly price.

Finally, a model that genuinely needs a full accelerator, or more than one, should keep having one. No partition spans accelerators.

Supported instances and Regions

GPU partitioning is available on the P4d, P5, G7, and G7e instance families. Support is at the family level, so smaller sizes within a family are covered.

It’s available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (Ireland).

Instance availability varies by Region, so confirm that your chosen instance type is offered in your Region and that you have endpoint usage quota for it.

Getting started

To partition a GPU endpoint, work out the memory and compute each of your model’s needs, pick the profiles that fit, declare a layout on your endpoint configuration, and deploy each model as an inference component that requests a profile from that layout. Nothing about how you invoke your models changes.

For the API reference, the full profile tables for each instance family, and a step-by-step walkthrough, see GPU partitioning in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide.

To try it yourself, run the GPU partitioning sample notebook, which deploys several models onto partitions of a single GPU endpoint.

The broader change is worth keeping in mind as you plan capacity. Every supported accelerator is now several sizes rather than one. Whether a partition of a newer GPU or a whole accelerator of an older one is the right unit for a given model is no longer a question you need to answer by rounding up. It’s one you can measure.

entries.title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick
entries.summary: As we built Amazon Quick, its agents grew from answering questions to taking actions, and the same primitives kept getting rebuilt under different names. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on — triggers, agents, capabilities, and learned context — found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When, What, Who, and How.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Taxonomy of agentic primitives in Amazon Quick

Over the past year, as we built Amazon Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user.

Take the user who says “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice.

This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When?, What?, Who?, and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it.

The framework at a glance

A trigger starts the work and carries the task (When and What), an agent takes it on (Who) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task (How). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more.

Triggers: What causes work to begin

Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task.

  • Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational.
  • Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive.
  • Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs.
  • Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook.

The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop).

Agents

We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor. It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things:

  • Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this.
  • Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next.
  • Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions.

Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform.

A consequence of this definition is that a user request “I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent, not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work.

Capabilities

Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract: how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance.

Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result.

Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure, so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost.

Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s.

Why skills and workflows outlast model improvements

A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and deterministic multi-service coordination. Nor are they fixed: a well-understood skill can tighten into a workflow (crystallization), a workflow that keeps hitting edge cases can loosen back into a skill (dissolution). This is done in Quick through our continuous learning framework, which we will describe in a future post.

What this means in practice

Return to “monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest”. Because these primitives compose, the same request can be met several valid ways:

  • A scheduled task with a one-line instruction, leaving the agent to figure out the rest.
  • The same task backed by a skill with explicit formatting rules and channel priorities.
  • The same task invoking a workflow with deterministic steps and error handling.

All three produce a daily digest on a schedule. What differs is the confidence contract. A user who trusts the agent wants the first, one burned by inconsistency the second, one running a compliance-sensitive process the third.

Learning shifts that trajectory over time. A task that starts as one sentence (“check my email for urgent items”) accumulates domain-bound learnings: effective queries, preferred formatting, and which senders matter. The tenth run is markedly better, with no one encoding that by hand. The right design is the simplest option that meets the user’s confidence requirement, with a path to graduate through autonomous learning when they need more.

Conclusion

The value of this agentic primitive taxonomy is that four plain questions, When, What, Who, and How, are enough to place any piece of agentic work, from a one-line chat request to a scheduled, compliance-grade process. Sharing one vocabulary lets builders reason about the system and lets the product hide complexity. Best of all, the user never has to learn any of it. They say what they want, and the system assembles the appropriate primitives to do their job.

Next in the series: the agentic operating system that builds on these primitives and powers Amazon Quick.

Keep exploring

  • Ready to try? Start with the Amazon Quick getting-started guide.

entries.title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
entries.summary: Learn how to build a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate that gives AI agents secure, metadata-driven access to an enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON file, with no per-dataset integration code.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate

Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort.

Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync.

In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment.

Problem statement and design goals

Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model.

Integration challenge at scale

Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table.

Design goals

We established four requirements:

  • Configuration-driven data lake access. Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code.
  • Agent-agnostic tool interfaces. Any MCP-compatible client can invoke the same tools.
  • Centralized permission enforcement. Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer.
  • Elastic infrastructure. The system scales with bursty AI workload patterns.

Solution overview

The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail.

Architecture walkthrough

The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazon DynamoDB and forwards requests through an internal Application Load Balancer to the MCP server layer, also on Amazon ECS Fargate. In the MCP server layer, an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction. On the right, the data layer holds the tool backends. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift run SQL queries against the data lake, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handles semantic search. Data ingestion into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the knowledge bases is handled by AWS Lambda. Each layer is described in detail in the sections that follow.

MCP client layer: Authentication and session management

A request flows from the client application through Amazon Route 53 for DNS resolution to an Application Load Balancer configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer forwards traffic to the Amazon ECS Fargate client service, which integrates with Amazon Cognito for JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Amazon DynamoDB for session storage.

A context mapping configuration drives this enrichment, scoping each query to only the relevant tables. In our testing, this scoping keeps end-to-end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range. The following example shows a context mapping configuration:

When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to those tables, reducing noise and improving SQL generation accuracy. Adding a new business domain requires only adding an entry to this mapping.

MCP server layer: Stateless execution with conversation state

The MCP server runs on its own ECS Fargate cluster, isolated from the client layer. Requests reach it through Amazon Route 53 and an internal Application Load Balancer in a private subnet. The server handles full orchestration including query analysis, tool selection, execution, and response generation. Through the MCP protocol endpoint (

/mcp
), a FastMCP-powered JSON-RPC interface, external MCP-compatible clients such as Amazon Q Developer or IDE extensions can discover and invoke tools directly.

Fargate tasks are stateless with conversation state persisted in DynamoDB, so tasks can be replaced or scaled without data loss. When a request arrives, the agent retrieves session history, analyzes user intent using Amazon Bedrock, discovers and invokes appropriate tools, and streams results back to the user.

Tools layer and metadata-driven data lake access

Each tool is registered with FastMCP and discoverable at runtime:

Sr.noToolBackendPurpose
1SQL query tools

Amazon Athena

Amazon Redshift

 SQL queries against any configured dataset in the data lake and Redshift
2Document and metadata searchAmazon Bedrock Knowledge BasesSemantic search over internal documentation, table metadata and team wikis
3Policy searchAmazon Bedrock Knowledge BasesSearch operational policies and standard procedures

The Athena query tools are the primary interface to the data lake. The agent first queries the metadata catalog to understand available schemas, generates an optimized SQL query through Amazon Bedrock, validates and auto-corrects the SQL for Athena compatibility, then executes it. Results flow back to the orchestrating agent for natural language synthesis.

Responsible AI controls

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to all LLM interactions and is designed to filter harmful content, enforce grounding checks, and help block prompt injection attempts. These guardrails operate as production controls at the MCP server layer, so every connected agent benefits from the same content safety policies regardless of how it connects. The Athena query tools enforce 

SELECT
-only queries, rejecting write operations at the tool level before they reach the data lake.

Knowledge base refresh layer: Dataset onboarding with a single JSON file

The entire system is built around configuration-driven extensibility. Adding a new dataset requires a metadata JSON file describing the table and an optional context mapping entry. The file captures the table’s schema, business context, and column-level semantics. It serves as the single source of truth that the AI agent uses to understand and query the dataset:

The 

business_description_for_the_table
field carries engine-specific query hints, such as “always use 
date()
to wrap string literals,” that reduce SQL validation failures. The 
column_details
field pairs each 
column_name [type]
with a natural language description and sample values, giving the agent both schema awareness and business semantics. The 
sample_values
field matters for accurate 
WHERE
clause generation because the agent learns real data patterns, for instance that 
warehouse_id
holds codes like 
FC-EAST-07
rather than spelled-out names like “East region facility.”

The pipeline picks up metadata files, generates vector embeddings with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and indexes them into Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Once indexed, the table is discoverable by all connected agents without manual re-indexing or server restarts.

To improve accuracy for specific applications, an engineer can optionally associate the dataset with a business context. This narrows the search scope, so the agent prioritizes the right tables. The following example shows a context mapping entry:

If no context is specified, the agent searches across all indexed tables. The context mapping reduces latency and improves SQL accuracy by limiting the search space. This scoping is optional and can be added at any time without modifying the metadata files themselves.

Putting it together: A query in action

When a user asks, “What were our top 10 highest-value orders last month?”, the client enriches the request with business context to narrow scope. The agent converts the question into a vector embedding, searches the metadata catalog for matching schemas, and selects the most relevant table via a lightweight LLM call.

Using the selected schema, column descriptions, and engine-specific query hints, the agent generates a SQL statement such as:

The SQL is validated and auto-corrected for engine compatibility, then executed against Amazon Athena. The agent formats the results into a natural language response and streams it back to the user. In our testing, this end-to-end flow completes within 15–20 seconds.

The same orchestration extends beyond pure SQL. Because document search is registered as another tool on the same server, the agent can answer questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single turn, such as “What was our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” For that request, the agent runs an Athena query for the return-rate figure and a Knowledge Bases document search for the analysis, then combines both into one response.

Security and multi-tenant access

That single-turn orchestration works only because every tool call passes through the same controlled gateway. The architecture uses layered security rather than a single enforcement point. The MCP server runs in private subnets behind an internal Application Load Balancer and is not reachable from the internet. Only the client layer, which sits behind a public-facing Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF, can route requests to it. Amazon Cognito validates user identity at the client layer, and only authenticated, token-bearing requests are forwarded downstream. At the tool level, the Athena query tools enforce 

SELECT
-only queries, rejecting write operations before they reach the data lake. All tool invocations are logged to Amazon CloudWatch with structured JSON, which gives security teams a single audit point for data access across every agent and application. This architecture is available in the AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases are available.

This centralized design is also what makes the server multi-tenant. Because the standardized 

/mcp
endpoint accepts any MCP-compatible client regardless of which LLM or orchestration framework it uses, multiple agents share the same tools and the same access controls. Adding a new agent requires only pointing it at the server endpoint, so onboarding another team extends the system without weakening or duplicating the security model.

Serverless infrastructure and scaling

Each layer scales through a mechanism suited to its workload pattern:

LayerScaling mechanismTrigger
Client (ECS Fargate)ECS Service Auto ScalingCPU utilization (50% threshold)
MCP Server (ECS Fargate)ECS Service Auto ScalingCPU/Memory utilization
AthenaServerless (automatic)Query concurrency
Amazon BedrockManaged service scalingInference requests

Amazon ECS Fargate provides serverless compute with no EC2 instances to manage. Downstream services (Athena, Bedrock) scale automatically, so the system handles a single query or hundreds of concurrent queries without configuration changes.

Use cases and extensions

This architecture supports several patterns beyond basic question-answering. Enterprise knowledge assistants can combine data lake queries with document search to answer complex questions spanning both structured data and unstructured knowledge, such as “What’s our return rate for Q4, and what does the product team’s analysis say about the root causes?” Internal analytics copilots let business users query the data lake conversationally without writing SQL, relying on the metadata descriptions and query hints to guide the agent toward accurate, performant query patterns.

The standardized 

/mcp
endpoint also supports multi-agent workflows. Multiple specialized agents for data analysis, document retrieval, and operational alerting can share the same MCP server, each accessing the full tool suite through a common protocol. Onboarding a new team’s data follows the same configuration-driven pattern. They add a metadata JSON file, and within one pipeline sync cycle their dataset is discoverable by every connected agent and application.

Conclusion

A centralized MCP server on Amazon ECS Fargate provides a scalable, secure gateway between AI agents and enterprise data lakes. The metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and the Model Context Protocol standard means any MCP-compatible client can connect without custom adapters.

The key architectural decision is separating the tool layer from the agent layer. Agents evolve rapidly, but data access patterns should outlive any single agent implementation. Treating extensibility as a configuration problem rather than a code problem accelerates onboarding.

To learn more, see Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate, Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases user guide, Amazon Athena, and the Model Context Protocol specification.

Next steps

We are extending this architecture in two directions. First, finer-grained access control where table owners can mark sensitive columns as restricted per permission group, and the agent automatically excludes those columns from generated SQL without prompt-level changes.

Second, closing the feedback loop so that when queries fail or produce low-confidence results, the system captures the failure pattern and surfaces targeted suggestions for improving column descriptions, adding query hints.

entries.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
entries.summary: In Part 1 you built one governed agent. Part 2 scales the pattern to an enterprise: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway becomes the single front door and redeems Okta's grant, Cedar policies bind each tool to the agent, a second agent runs on Amazon EKS, and AgentCore Observability traces every allow and deny beside Okta's log in Amazon CloudWatch.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2

In Part 1, you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server.

The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools:

What Part 1 doesWhy it stops scalingWhat Part 2 does instead
The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directlyN agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs itAgents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry
The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secretEvery agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reachThe Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions
Each MCP server carries the same 
groups
check in its own code		 The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one placeOne default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run

In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant.

What changes from Part 1

The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions.

  • The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1.
  • The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG.
  • Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs.
  • Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target.
  • For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG.
  • The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an 
    authz.check
    span.
  • Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.

The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway.

Prerequisites

In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following:

PrerequisiteNeeded for
eksctl, kubectl, and DockerThe second agent on Amazon EKS
Okta Log StreamingOkta’s System Log in CloudWatch
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissionsAgentCore Gateways and policy engines, Amazon EKS clusters, CloudWatch log groups, and Amazon EventBridge rules

The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.

Create a Gateway that accepts the ID-JAG

The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and 

allowedClients
pins it to one agent:

Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer.

Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses 

TOKEN_EXCHANGE
through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange:

Figure 3 shows a target configured this way.

Three details matter here. First, as in Part 1, the target’s scopes must equal the ID-JAG’s. Second, give each target a static tool schema (

listingMode
set to 
DEFAULT
with an inline 
mcpToolSchema
), so the tool names your Cedar policies reference are fixed when you write them. In our tests, policies that name tools also couldn’t attach to dynamically listed targets. Third, the Gateway pages 
tools/list
by target, so your client must follow the pagination cursor, or tools from later targets disappear. AgentCore Identity keeps the token from the Gateway’s exchange, so one single-use ID-JAG serves every tool call in a session. In our tests, it also opened a second session within its 5-minute life.

Because a credential provider authenticates as one Okta agent, give each agent its own Gateway and provider. Sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain takes a different route, in which a Gateway interceptor performs both exchanges itself.

Bind tools to agents with Cedar

Attach a Policy in AgentCore engine to the Gateway in 

ENFORCE
mode, and write permit-only policies. Cedar exposes JWT claims as tags. A policy that reads a missing tag errors and is skipped. A skipped 
permit
grants nothing, so default deny holds, but a skipped 
forbid
blocks nothing. Guard each tag with 
hasTag
:

The scope tag holds the ID-JAG’s space-separated 

scope
claim, so the four conditions match 
xaa:write
only as a whole entry. A scope such as 
xaa:write-admin
doesn’t match. A matching policy, written the same way, permits the read tools with 
xaa:read
. Check that every policy is 
ACTIVE
before you attach the engine: an engine whose policies failed to create leaves the Gateway denying every call. Cedar binds tools to the agent and its delegated scope, and the MCP server still decides each user’s authority from the 
groups
claim, as in Part 1.

Point the agent at the Gateway

Agent A now forwards its inbound ID-JAG to the Gateway instead of calling AgentCore Identity itself:

Remove the Part 1 AgentCore Identity statements from the agent’s execution role. That’s the only change to the role, which now holds no token-exchange or secret permissions, because the Gateway’s role holds the permission to exchange tokens. Keep 

allowedClients
on the runtime’s authorizer.

Run a second agent on Amazon EKS

Our second agent, a reporting agent, runs the same code on Amazon EKS with its own Okta registration. Its resource connection allows only 

xaa:read
, and it has its own Gateway and credential provider. EKS Pod Identity gives the pod an IAM role that can invoke models and write its own logs and traces, and nothing else. The AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK exports its traces. The agents-on-eks sample shows the Pod Identity setup.

Outside AgentCore runtime, no authorizer sits in front of the pod, so the agent validates the ID-JAG before a model call. It checks the signature, issuer, audience, token type 

oauth-id-jag+jwt
, expiry, and that 
client_id
is its own. If you kept the Part 1 agent check in the MCP servers, add agent B’s client ID to 
REGISTERED_AGENTS
. Two settings tripped us up. The EKS Auto Mode general-purpose node pool runs only amd64, so build multi-architecture images. And the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, binds to 
localhost
unless you set 
DOCKER_CONTAINER=true
.

Trace every decision with AgentCore Observability

The spans in this section are AgentCore Observability, the component in Figure 1 that sits between the agents and CloudWatch. Runtime, Gateway, Identity, and Policy emit OpenTelemetry spans for each hop without code changes, after you turn on Transaction Search and trace delivery. Your own services add theirs with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). CloudWatch Transaction Search collects them, the AgentCore console reads them as agent traces, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni reads the same spans as 

traces.default
, which is what lets one query put them beside Okta’s events.

One tool call therefore produces this chain of spans, each naming the control that made a decision:

SpanEmitted byWhat it records
AgentCore.Gateway.InboundAuth
 GatewayWhether the inbound ID-JAG was issued to this agent
AgentCore.Policy.AuthorizeAction
 PolicyThe Cedar decision for this tool
AgentCore.Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken
 IdentityBinding the agent’s workload identity to the user
AgentCore.Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token
 IdentityRedeeming the ID-JAG at Okta for a scoped access token
AgentCore.Gateway.InvokeTool
 GatewayThe tool call and its outcome
authz.check
 The MCP server (ADOT)The user’s groups, the agent, the decision, and the reason

Okta’s System Log is the one record AWS can’t emit, so you bring it in. Figure 4 shows both paths meeting in Omni.

To set it up:

  • Turn on CloudWatch Transaction Search, turn on trace delivery for each Gateway (see this sample script), and add ADOT to the BFF and the MCP servers. The task manager writes each decision, the user, and the agent onto an 
    authz.check
    span.
  • In Okta, add a Log Stream for Amazon EventBridge. Okta delivers each event to a partner event bus in your account, and a rule writes it to a CloudWatch Logs log group. In our tests, events arrived about 1 second after Okta published them. Each ID-JAG grant event names the agent as the actor, the user as a target, and the granted scopes and resource connection.
  • Set up an Omni space in the account and AWS Region, add the Okta log group to the CloudWatch Dataset integration, and save a view, 
    view.xaa_authz_decisions
    , over the 
    authz.check
    spans.

One query then joins each ID-JAG grant to the decisions it led to:

For Alice, the result shows Okta granting the task agent 

xaa:read xaa:write
for her, then the MCP server denying her 
create_task
16.7 seconds later and allowing 
list_tasks
after that, as Figure 5 shows.

Each request is also one trace, from the BFF through the agent, the Gateway’s identity and policy checks, and the MCP server’s decision, as Figure 6 shows. Omni marks the trace as a fault because the agent’s 

create_task
call returned the denial.

Two instrumentation details matter. ADOT finds the Region and signs its exports through 

botocore
, so add 
botocore
to services that lack it. Until we did, our MCP servers exported no spans. And ADOT’s agent mode turns off instrumentation for HTTP client libraries such as 
requests
and 
urllib3
by default, so set 
OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS
in your BFF to override that default with a list that leaves out the BFF’s HTTP client (
requests
, in ours), or its trace context won’t reach the agent.

Validate the results

We ran each check through both Gateways with the users from Part 1. Each session listed the tools, then called 

list_tasks
, 
create_task
, and an employee lookup:
Caller and pathTools listed
create_task
 Reads
Alice, agent A, Gateway A6Denied by the MCP server: requires 
xaa-writers
 Allowed
Bob, agent A, Gateway A6CreatedAllowed
Carol, agent A, Gateway A6Denied by the MCP server: no 
groups
claim		 Allowed
Bob, agent B, Gateway B4: Cedar hid the write toolsRefused by the Gateway: “No policy applies to the request (denied by default)”Allowed

Through the deployed agents, the results matched: agent A denied Alice and Carol and created Bob’s task, and agent B told Bob it had no tool to create tasks. The same user got different authority through different agents, and Okta decided it.

These requests stopped at the front door:

RequestResponse
Agent B’s ID-JAG at Gateway A, or agent A’s at Gateway BHTTP 403, MCP error -32002 
insufficient_scope
An Okta access token instead of an ID-JAGHTTP 403, the same error
No tokenHTTP 401, “Missing Bearer token”
Agent A’s ID-JAG sent to agent B on EKSRefused in 98 milliseconds, before a model call: “issued to a different agent”

The Gateway returns the same generic error for a wrong agent and for the wrong token type, so check your configuration against the token’s 

client_id
and 
aud
when you see it.

The Gateway’s identity and policy work is small next to the tool itself. Medians and 90th percentiles from 24 hours of Gateway A spans in Omni:

Spanp50p90
Gateway.InboundAuth
 34 ms69 ms
Identity.Authorize
 25 ms60 ms
Identity.GetWorkloadAccessToken
 48 ms94 ms
Identity.GetResourceOauth2Token
 70 ms439 ms
Policy.AuthorizeAction
(Cedar, per call)		 47 ms56 ms
Policy.PartiallyAuthorizeActions
(Cedar, per tool listing)		 65 ms75 ms
Gateway.TargetInvocation
(the MCP server on AgentCore runtime)		 5,565 ms6,273 ms

The identity and policy spans for one tool call sum to about 0.2 seconds at their medians, and the MCP server’s own 

authz.check
span took under 1 millisecond. Gateway B showed the same pattern, with 
GetResourceOauth2Token
at 408 milliseconds at the median.

Cross App Access or per-user consent

XAA applies where the target application’s authorization server accepts an ID-JAG. There, your Okta administrator decides which agent may act for which users, users see no consent prompt, and Okta evaluates policy each time a token is requested. Applications with their own authorization servers, such as GitHub, rely on each user’s own OAuth consent instead. Figure 7 compares the two, as we measured them.

We deployed the AWS sample 07-consent-portal-auth-code-flow-targets beside our stack, with Okta signing users in to an AgentCore Identity consent portal and a GitHub target on its own Gateway. Alice connected a GitHub test account through the portal, and Bob never connected one. The post Manage end-user OAuth consent for AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore describes this lane in full. Here’s what we observed:

ActionNext GitHub tool call
Alice consented in the portalReturned her GitHub identity
Bob, who never consentedMCP error -32042 with an AgentCore authorization URL
Alice suspended in Okta, earlier token reusedStill worked: the Gateway checks the inbound token’s signature and expiry, and that token lived 1 hour
Alice suspended, new sign-inRefused
Alice unsuspendedWorked with no new consent
Alice’s grant disconnected through the consent portal’s APINot connected, then -32042 again

The two lanes revoke differently. In XAA, Okta’s controls stop the next ID-JAG mint, and issued tokens expire within about 5 minutes. In the consent lane, Okta controls only sign-in: the stored grant outlived the suspension and stayed until we disconnected it. Choose per target application, not once for the enterprise.

Where this pattern applies

In media and entertainment, the fleet arrives quickly. A studio or streaming or games organization has agents for production tracking, title and asset metadata, rights and localization, and viewer or player support, each sitting in front of a different system with its own authorization model and its own auditors. The question isn’t whether one agent can be governed. It’s whether the hundredth one is governed the same way, and whether an administrator can still answer which agents reach which systems for which users.

Nothing here is specific to that industry. The agent is an identity in your IdP, the target is an OAuth 2.0 authorization server, and the Gateway is where authorization is decided. Teams in financial services, healthcare, and the public sector put different resources behind the same front door and get the same audit trail.

What’s next: observability and evaluations

This post uses AgentCore Observability for one purpose: to prove that each allow and deny traces back to a control. There’s more in it than that, and it’s a body of work in its own right. The spans already carry the model and tool latency behind every governance decision, Transaction Search can alert on a spike in denials, and AgentCore evaluations can score an agent’s behavior against your own criteria, online for live traffic or on demand over a chosen set of spans. A later post takes that up: what to measure on a governed agent, which evaluators catch an agent that reports success after a refused tool call, and how to run both without turning your traces into your largest bill.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the Part 2 resources, then follow the cleanup steps in Part 1:

  • Delete the Amazon EKS cluster (
    eksctl delete cluster
    ) and its Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository.
  • Delete the Gateways and their targets, then the Policy in AgentCore engines, and then agent B’s credential provider.
  • Delete the CloudWatch Omni space and domain, the Dataset integration, the Amazon EventBridge rule and partner event bus, and the CloudWatch log groups.
  • If you deployed sample 07, follow its cleanup steps.
  • Delete the IAM roles and policies you created.
  • In Okta, delete the log stream, and deactivate and delete agent B and its linked app.

Conclusion

In this post, you moved the Part 1 solution from a topology that suits a few agents and tools to one that holds up across many. The Gateway became the single front door and redeemed Okta’s grant, so the agents held no tool credentials. Cedar policies evaluated by Policy in AgentCore replaced the check copied into each server. A second agent on Amazon EKS joined under its own Okta identity. And AgentCore Observability, with Okta’s System Log beside it in CloudWatch Omni, traced each allow and deny back to the agent, the user, and the control that decided it. The governance mechanism didn’t change, which is the point: only the topology around it did.

To get started, explore the AgentCore samples and Okta’s Cross App Access documentation. For plain token exchange through a Gateway, read Implement on-behalf-of token exchange for multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

entries.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
entries.summary: An AI agent that acts for a user raises an identity question that per-app OAuth and service accounts leave open: which agent may act for which user, and how you stop it. In this first post of two, you build a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that governs access through Okta Cross App Access and AgentCore Identity, and enforces each user's authority.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1

An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end.

In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch.

Solution overview

Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime.

Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this:

  • The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app.
  • For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes.
  • The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent.
  • The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens.
  • The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups.
  • The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool.

Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need the following:

PrerequisiteWhat we used
An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon BedrockUS West (Oregon)
An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers)An Okta Integrator Free Plan org
Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCorePython 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissionsPermission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles

The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it.

Register the agent in Okta

Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.

  • Create a custom authorization server for the resource application with the audience 
    api://task-manager
    and the custom scopes 
    xaa:read
    and 
    xaa:write
    . Request only the resource’s custom scopes: Okta rejects an ID-JAG request that includes OpenID Connect scopes such as 
    openid
    or 
    profile
    (
    invalid_scope
    ), so a request needs at least one custom scope and no OpenID Connect scopes.
  • Add a 
    groups
    claim to its access tokens, filtered to groups that start with 
    xaa-
    . This claim carries each user’s authority to the tools.
  • In the Admin Console, go to Directory > AI Agents, choose Register AI agent and then Register manually, optionally assign an owner, and create a linked OpenID Connect app. On Client registration, choose Client secret, generate a secret, and then activate the agent. The agent and the app share one client ID, and that app must sign your users in: an ID token from another app fails the exchange with “the client application is not registered for delegation to this agent.”
  • On the agent’s Resource connections tab, connect it to the authorization server, limited to the scopes it needs, as Figure 3 shows.
  • Add an access policy rule to the custom authorization server that allows the agent’s JWT Bearer grant, with a 5-minute access token lifetime. Without the grant type, the second exchange fails with 
    no_matching_policy
    , and the lifetime bounds how long a revoked delegation keeps working.
  • Assign the users or groups who might act through the agent. They sign in through the linked app, so give it an app sign-in policy that admits them with the authenticators they’ve enrolled. In our sandbox org, the linked app had its own policy with a rule for the test group. For real users, apply your organization’s policy, including multifactor authentication.

Okta’s Cross App Access guide covers the console steps, and the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain scripts the authorization server and its JWT bearer policy. The BFF then requests the ID-JAG, authenticated as the agent:

The AWS sample 

06-okta-xaa
sends the same request in Python (agent/xaa_client.py). The BFF authenticates as the agent, so store the agent’s client secret in AWS Secrets Manager rather than in code or configuration files.

Set up AgentCore Identity

AgentCore Identity holds three things for this solution, and your agent code doesn’t see the client secret or call Okta’s token endpoint:

Part of AgentCore IdentityWhat it holdsWho creates it
Workload identityThe agent’s identity on AWS, bound to the signed-in user for each requestAgentCore runtime, for each agent runtime
OAuth2 credential providerThe agent’s Okta client ID and secret, and the grant to useYou, once per Okta agent
Token vaultThe access tokens the provider obtainsAgentCore Identity

Create the credential provider

The credential provider performs the second exchange. Point it at the custom authorization server, authenticate it as the AI agent, and set the on-behalf-of grant to 

JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT
, which AgentCore Identity sends as 
jwt-bearer
with the ID-JAG as the assertion:

Okta binds both exchanges to the client named in the ID-JAG, so each Okta agent needs its own provider: when we redeemed one agent’s ID-JAG as another, Okta refused with “The ‘client_id’ in the JWT Bearer Grant must match the ‘client_id’ used to authenticate the client.” AgentCore Identity keeps the secret in a service-managed AWS Secrets Manager secret, which you rotate with 

update-oauth2-credential-provider
. If your team already manages the client secret in Secrets Manager, you can reference that secret’s ARN instead. AgentCore Identity reads the client secret from it, so you can rotate the secret without updating the provider (see Reference your own AWS Secrets Manager secrets in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity). To avoid a shared secret, authenticate with a private key instead. See Authenticate with Private Key JWT using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. Figure 4 shows the provider in the AgentCore console.

Use the workload identity that AgentCore runtime manages

AgentCore runtime creates and manages a workload identity for each agent runtime. When a request passes the runtime’s JWT authorizer, the runtime gets a workload access token for that workload identity and the inbound token’s issuer and subject, and passes it to your code. AgentCore Identity then uses the ID-JAG behind it as the assertion for the exchange.

The AgentCore Python SDK keeps the workload access token in 

BedrockAgentCoreContext
, not in the request headers that your entrypoint receives. Our first version looked for it in the headers, found nothing, and fell back to its own 
GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT
call with a second workload identity, on all 21 requests we checked. Read it from the context instead:

AgentCore Identity keeps the access token in its token vault for the rest of the request. Across 10 requests, the agent’s first call redeemed the ID-JAG in about half a second (see the latency table in Validate the results), and the second, for the other MCP server, returned the same token in a median of 58 milliseconds without redeeming the single-use ID-JAG again. A new ID-JAG for the same user got a new token, so each request reflects Okta’s latest decision. The sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain reads the workload access token the same way (agent/agent.py).

Scope the agent’s role to its workload identity and provider

AgentCore Identity doesn’t bind workload identities to credential providers in the same account. The agent’s IAM role does, so scope it to the agent’s own workload identity and provider, and to that provider’s secret:

Take the workload identity’s name from 

workloadIdentityDetails
in 
GetAgentRuntime
, and the provider’s ARN from 
credentialProviderArn
: the segment is 
oauth2credentialprovider
, and with the hyphenated form every call failed with 
AccessDeniedException
. The role needs no 
GetWorkloadAccessToken
permission, because the runtime gets that token, not the agent. Our tests passed with only these two statements.

Deploy the agent on AgentCore runtime

Configure the agent runtime’s inbound authorizer to accept only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, and its audience is the resource’s custom authorization server. In 

agentcore.json
:

allowedClients
matches the 
client_id
claim that an ID-JAG carries. Without it, the runtime admitted another agent’s ID-JAG with HTTP 200 and the request failed later, at the exchange. With it, the runtime refused that token with HTTP 401.

Besides the policy from the previous section, the execution role needs 

bedrock:InvokeModel
and 
bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream
. It needs no 
bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime
permission for the MCP servers: each runs on AgentCore runtime behind its own JWT authorizer, with the custom authorization server as issuer and 
api://task-manager
as audience, so the agent calls it with the Okta access token as a bearer token, not with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).

Enforce each user’s authority in the MCP server

The resource connection sets the scopes for every user of an agent, so all three test users received 

xaa:read xaa:write
, and per-user authority travels in the 
groups
claim instead: Alice’s token carried 
xaa-readers
, Bob’s 
xaa-writers
, and Carol’s had none.

The task manager checks two things: it accepts only tokens a registered agent obtained, and it allows a write only when the group and the scope are both present:

Both checks close gaps we found: a write check that allowed tokens without a 

groups
claim let Carol, who belongs to neither group, create tasks, and before 
_require_agent
a plain token-exchange token, issued to a service app with no 
act
claim, created a task for Bob. The server can read the claims without verifying the token again only because the runtime’s JWT authorizer already verified it. A server without that authorizer in front of it must check the signature, issuer, audience, and expiry itself, as the Part 2 agent on Amazon EKS does.

Validate the results

We ran every check against the deployed solution. Alice, Bob, and Carol each asked the agent to create a task and then list the project’s tasks:

The token that AgentCore Identity returned matched one we redeemed directly at Okta, claim for claim:
